hypotheses.title: RedstoneNAVFeed.setPrice is callable by anyone
hypotheses.description: The `setPrice(uint256)` function has no access control modifier at all. Any external account can overwrite the NAV price used by `iTryIssuer` for minting, redemption, and yield calculations. The real Redstone consumer was commented out, leaving a fully open setter.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `RedstoneNAVFeed.setPrice(1)` (or any arbitrary value). 2) Attacker calls `iTryIssuer.mintITRY` with a tiny DLF amount; since `iTRYAmount = netDlfAmount * navPrice / 1e18`, a huge navPrice mints enormous iTRY. 3) Attacker redeems or sells the inflated iTRY, or sets navPrice to 0 to brick redemptions.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of protocol solvency — attacker mints arbitrary iTRY backed by nothing, drains collateral on redemption, or freezes all redemptions by setting price to 0.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the mock setter or gate it behind a trusted oracle role; restore the real Redstone consumer before deployment.

hypotheses.title: processAccumulatedYield mints yield based on manipulable oracle price
hypotheses.description: Yield is computed as `_totalDLFUnderCustody * navPrice / 1e18 - _totalIssuedITry` and minted to the yield receiver. The oracle is a mock with a public `setPrice` (RedstoneNAVFeed.setPrice) and no access control, so anyone can push the NAV price arbitrarily high. There is no TWAP, no deviation bound, and no check that the price is fresh.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor calls RedstoneNAVFeed.setPrice(hugeValue) to inflate NAV, then calls iTryIssuer.processAccumulatedYield() (if they hold YIELD_DISTRIBUTOR_ROLE — but even without it, the inflated price persists and any subsequent legitimate call mints an inflated yield). Alternatively, the attacker front-runs a legitimate yield distribution with an inflated price so the minted yield is far larger than real appreciation.
hypotheses.impact: Excess iTRY minted to yield receiver, diluting all iTRY holders and breaking the 1:1 collateral backing; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a tamper-resistant oracle (Redstone with signed payloads), add deviation/TWAP bounds, and restrict setPrice to a trusted updater with staleness checks.

hypotheses.title: iTry.addBlacklistAddress loop uses uint8 index, overflows for >255 users
hypotheses.description: The loop `for (uint8 i = 0; i < users.length; i++)` uses a `uint8` counter. If `users.length > 255`, the loop will overflow `i` back to 0 and run indefinitely (or until gas exhaustion), reverting the entire transaction. This means a blacklist manager cannot blacklist more than 255 addresses in a single call, and any attempt to do so reverts, potentially blocking the ability to blacklist a large batch of malicious actors.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A blacklist manager attempts to blacklist 256+ addresses in one call. 2. The `uint8 i` overflows at 255, causing an infinite loop or revert. 3. The blacklist operation fails, leaving malicious actors unblacklisted.
hypotheses.impact: Inability to blacklist large batches of addresses, potentially allowing malicious actors to continue operating. Also affects `removeBlacklistAddress`, `addWhitelistAddress`, and `removeWhitelistAddress` in the same file.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the loop counter to `uint256` in all four functions.

hypotheses.title: FastAccessVault.rebalanceFunds is callable by anyone
hypotheses.description: `rebalanceFunds()` has no access modifier, so any external caller can trigger it. When the vault balance exceeds the target, it transfers the excess DLF directly to `custodian`. The custodian address is set by the owner, but the trigger is fully permissionless, allowing an attacker to force the vault to dump its buffer to the custodian at will.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes vault balance above target (e.g., after a large mint). 2) Attacker calls `rebalanceFunds()`. 3) Vault transfers the entire excess to `custodian`, leaving only the minimum/target balance. 4) Attacker then triggers a redemption that requires buffer liquidity, forcing the slow custodian path or reverting.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on instant redemptions; buffer drained to custodian on attacker's schedule, breaking the fast-access guarantee and potentially causing user redemptions to fail or be delayed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `rebalanceFunds()` to the owner or issuer contract, or make it a keeper-only function with rate limiting.

hypotheses.title: RedstoneNAVFeed.price() returns uninitialized zero, no staleness check
hypotheses.description: The oracle is a mock that simply returns a storage variable `_price` with no initialization, no timestamp, no round validation, and no staleness check. Any consumer (iTryIssuer.previewMint/previewRedeem/processAccumulatedYield) reads this value directly. If `_price` is zero (default) or stale, downstream math either reverts or produces incorrect conversions.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls iTryIssuer.mintITRY/redeemITRY while the oracle returns a stale or zero price. Because iTryIssuer only checks `navPrice == 0` in some paths (previewMint/previewRedeem do not), a stale non-zero price lets the attacker mint iTRY at an outdated (higher) NAV or redeem at an outdated (lower) NAV, extracting value from the protocol.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong mint/redeem amounts, potential protocol insolvency as collateral accounting diverges from real NAV.
hypotheses.recommendation: Integrate the real Redstone consumer with timestamp/round validation and revert on stale or zero prices; add a max-age check in iTryIssuer before using oracle.price().

hypotheses.title: iTry.initialize can be front-run on proxy deployment
hypotheses.description: `initialize(address admin, address minterContract)` is `public` with only the `initializer` modifier. If the proxy is deployed and `initialize` is not called atomically in the same transaction, any external actor can call it first and become `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` and `MINTER_CONTRACT`. The constructor only calls `_disableInitializers()` on the implementation, not the proxy.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Deployer deploys the ERC1967 proxy pointing at the iTry implementation. 2) Before the deployer's `initialize` tx lands, attacker front-runs with `initialize(attacker, attacker)`. 3) Attacker now holds admin and minter roles, can mint unlimited iTRY, blacklist users, and update transfer state.
hypotheses.impact: Total takeover of the iTRY token — unlimited minting, blacklisting of any user, and control of transfer state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deploy and initialize atomically (e.g., via a factory or `initialize` call inside the proxy constructor), or use OpenZeppelin's `Initializable` with an atomic deploy pattern.

hypotheses.title: previewMint/previewRedeem use oracle.price() without zero check
hypotheses.description: previewMint and previewRedeem call `oracle.price()` and immediately divide/multiply without checking for zero. previewRedeem divides by `navPrice`, so a zero price causes a division-by-zero revert; previewMint multiplies by zero and returns 0, silently misleading integrators. The state-changing mintFor/redeemFor do check, but the preview functions do not, creating inconsistent behavior for callers that rely on previews.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted integrator or frontend calls previewRedeem while the oracle is momentarily zero (e.g., during a Redstone update window or misconfiguration), causing a revert that can be used to grief or to misprice off-chain quotes; previewMint returning 0 can be used to trick downstream contracts that trust the preview.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on preview paths, incorrect off-chain pricing, potential integration losses if a contract trusts previewMint's zero output.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (navPrice == 0) revert InvalidNAVPrice(navPrice);` in both previewMint and previewRedeem.

hypotheses.title: iTryIssuer.redeemFor burns user tokens before checking buffer, can revert after burn
hypotheses.description: In `redeemFor`, the function calls `_burn(msg.sender, iTRYAmount)` before checking the buffer balance and before calling `_redeemFromVault` or `_redeemFromCustodian`. If the subsequent call to `liquidityVault.processTransfer` reverts (e.g., due to insufficient buffer balance or a transfer failure), the entire transaction reverts, including the burn. However, if the burn succeeds and the subsequent transfer fails silently (e.g., in `_redeemFromCustodian` which only emits events), the user's tokens are burned but they receive no assets. This is a critical issue because `_redeemFromCustodian` does not actually transfer assets; it only emits events for off-chain processing. If the custodian fails to process the transfer, the user's tokens are burned with no recourse.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User calls `redeemFor` with a large amount. 2. Buffer is insufficient, so `_redeemFromCustodian` is called. 3. `_burn` burns the user's iTRY tokens. 4. `_redeemFromCustodian` only emits events; no actual transfer occurs. 5. If the custodian does not process the transfer, the user loses their tokens without receiving assets.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds if the custodian fails to process the transfer. The user's tokens are burned, but they receive no assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure that the custodian transfer is atomic or implement a mechanism to revert the burn if the custodian transfer fails.

hypotheses.title: wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake trusts user field without verifying spoke sender
hypotheses.description: `_handleUnstake` uses `unstakeMsg.user` directly as the address whose cooldown is unstaked, and only checks that the message came from a configured peer (`_origin.srcEid`). It never verifies that `unstakeMsg.user` equals the actual sender on the spoke chain (the `UnstakeMessenger` encodes `msg.sender` as `user`, but the hub does not re-derive or bind this to `_origin.sender`). Any peer that can craft a message with an arbitrary `user` field can force-unstake that user's cooldown.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls or compromises a spoke-chain peer (or finds a path where the peer is a contract that forwards arbitrary payloads). 2) Attacker sends a LayerZero message with `msgType = MSG_TYPE_UNSTAKE` and `unstakeMsg.user = victim`. 3) Hub `_lzReceive` accepts it because `_origin.srcEid` matches the configured peer. 4) `unstakeThroughComposer(victim)` is called, draining the victim's cooldown.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized unstaking of any user's cooldown entitlement; loss of funds / forced liquidation of staking positions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind `unstakeMsg.user` to the actual spoke sender (e.g., require `_origin.sender` to be the `UnstakeMessenger` and re-derive the user from a signed/authenticated field), or include the user in the signed payload and verify it on the hub.

hypotheses.title: Fast redeem fee calculation can cause share accounting mismatch
hypotheses.description: `_redeemWithFee` computes `feeAssets = (assets * fastRedeemFeeInBPS) / BASIS_POINTS` and then `feeShares = previewWithdraw(feeAssets)`. It then calls `_withdraw` twice: once for the fee portion (`feeAssets`, `feeShares`) and once for the net portion (`netAssets`, `netShares`). The sum of `feeShares + netShares` may not equal the original `shares` due to rounding in `previewWithdraw`. Specifically, `previewWithdraw(feeAssets)` rounds up, so `feeShares` can be larger than the proportional share of `feeAssets`. Then `netShares = shares - feeShares` may be smaller than the shares corresponding to `netAssets`. This means the user burns `shares` total, but the vault's internal accounting may attribute slightly different asset amounts to the fee and net portions. Over many transactions, this can lead to a drift between `totalAssets()` and the sum of individual share values. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly fast-redeeming tiny amounts to accumulate rounding errors in their favor.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker with a large share balance repeatedly calls `fastRedeem` with amounts chosen so that `previewWithdraw(feeAssets)` rounds up significantly relative to `feeAssets`. Each call, the attacker receives `netAssets = assets - feeAssets` but burns `netShares = shares - feeShares` where `feeShares` is rounded up. If `feeShares` is rounded up, `netShares` is smaller, meaning the attacker burns fewer shares than the proportional value of `netAssets`. Over many iterations, the attacker extracts value from the vault at the expense of other stakers.
hypotheses.impact: The vault's share-to-asset ratio drifts, causing other stakers to lose a small amount of value per fast-redeem. With enough iterations, this can be significant.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `feeShares` using `previewWithdraw` and then set `netShares = shares - feeShares`, but ensure that `netAssets` is recomputed as `previewRedeem(netShares)` to maintain consistency, or use a single `_withdraw` call and transfer the fee separately.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger refunds excess msg.value to user but hub may not receive enough for return trip
hypotheses.description: In `unstake`, the user provides `returnTripAllocation` as a parameter and sends `msg.value`. The contract quotes the spoke→hub fee with `returnTripAllocation` embedded in the options, validates `msg.value >= fee.nativeFee`, and sends the message. The excess `msg.value - fee.nativeFee` is refunded to the user. However, the `returnTripAllocation` is forwarded to the hub as native value via `addExecutorLzReceiveOption`. The hub receives exactly `returnTripAllocation` and uses it for the return trip. If the actual return trip fee on the hub is higher than `returnTripAllocation` (e.g., due to gas price fluctuations), the hub's `_send` will revert or the return trip will fail. The user is responsible for providing a sufficient `returnTripAllocation`, but there is no validation that `returnTripAllocation` is sufficient for the actual return trip. The `quoteUnstakeWithBuffer` function applies a buffer to the total fee, but the buffer is applied to the spoke→hub fee, not to `returnTripAllocation`. So the user could provide a `returnTripAllocation` that is too low, and the hub would not have enough native value to pay for the return trip.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user calls `unstake` with a `returnTripAllocation` that is lower than the actual hub→spoke fee. The spoke→hub message succeeds, the hub receives the insufficient `returnTripAllocation`, and when the hub tries to send the return trip, it fails due to insufficient native value. The user's funds are stuck on the hub (the unstaked iTRY is sent to the user on the spoke chain, but the return trip fails, so the user doesn't receive the iTRY). The user loses the gas paid for the spoke→hub message and the `returnTripAllocation`.
hypotheses.impact: The user's unstaked iTRY is stuck on the hub, and the user loses the fees paid. The user cannot recover the funds without another crosschain message.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `returnTripAllocation` is at least the quoted return trip fee, or apply the buffer to `returnTripAllocation` as well.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger.unstake trusts user-supplied returnTripAllocation
hypotheses.description: The user supplies `returnTripAllocation` (the native value forwarded to the hub for the return leg) with no minimum or maximum bound and no validation against the actual hub→spoke fee. The contract embeds it into LayerZero options via `addExecutorLzReceiveOption(LZ_RECEIVE_GAS, uint128(returnTripAllocation))`. If the user under-funds the return leg, the hub-side `_send` for the return trip will fail or the user will receive less than expected; if over-funded, the excess is stuck on the hub (refunded only to wiTryVaultComposer, not the user).
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls unstake with a tiny returnTripAllocation (e.g., 1 wei). The hub receives the message, calls `unstakeThroughComposer`, then `_send(ASSET_OFT, ...)` with `MessagingFee(msg.value, 0)` where msg.value is the tiny allocation — the LayerZero send reverts or the user's assets are stranded on the hub. The user's iTRY is already burned on the hub side, so they lose funds.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (iTRY burned on hub, no return transfer), or assets stuck on hub composer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `returnTripAllocation >= quoteUnstakeReturn(...)` computed on-chain, or have the hub verify the received native value covers the return fee before burning.

hypotheses.title: StakediTryCrosschain.unstakeThroughComposer allows anyone to trigger unstake for any user
hypotheses.description: The `unstakeThroughComposer` function is callable by any address with `COMPOSER_ROLE`. It takes a `receiver` parameter and withdraws the cooldown assets for that receiver to `msg.sender` (the composer). If a malicious composer (or a compromised composer) calls this for a user whose cooldown has ended, the assets are sent to the composer, not the user. While the composer is trusted, the function does not verify that the caller is acting on behalf of the receiver, and the assets are sent to `msg.sender` rather than the receiver. This means a malicious composer can steal the user's cooled-down assets.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User initiates cooldown via `cooldownSharesByComposer`, setting `cooldowns[user].underlyingAmount`. 2. After cooldown ends, a malicious composer calls `unstakeThroughComposer(user)`. 3. The function withdraws assets from the silo to `msg.sender` (the malicious composer). 4. The user's cooldown is reset, and the user loses their assets.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds if a composer is malicious or compromised. The user's cooled-down assets are sent to the composer instead of the user.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send the withdrawn assets directly to the `receiver` instead of `msg.sender`, or require that the caller is the receiver.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger.unstake lacks nonce/deadline; replayable cross-chain unstake
hypotheses.description: The `UnstakeMessage` payload only contains `user` and `extraOptions`; there is no nonce, deadline, or per-request identifier. The hub-side `wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake` processes any message from the trusted peer and calls `unstakeThroughComposer(user)`, which drains the user's cooldown entitlement. Because the payload is deterministic for a given user, a captured LayerZero message (or a re-delivered one) can be replayed to trigger additional unstake attempts against the same user's cooldown state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a legitimate `UnstakeRequested` message on the spoke chain (or obtains the raw payload via mempool/relayer). 2) Attacker re-submits the identical payload through the LayerZero endpoint (or via a compromised/duplicated relayer path) to the hub. 3) Hub `_lzReceive` decodes the same `UnstakeMessage` and calls `unstakeThroughComposer(user)` again. 4) If the user has re-accumulated cooldown entitlement (e.g., after a new cooldown), the attacker can force an unstake without the user's fresh consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized forced unstaking of a user's cooldown entitlement; potential loss of funds if the user intended to keep the position, and griefing/DoS on the user's staking strategy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a per-user nonce (and optionally a deadline) in `UnstakeMessage`, track consumed nonces on the hub, and reject duplicates.

hypotheses.title: processAccumulatedYield mints unbacked yield enabling double redemption
hypotheses.description: `processAccumulatedYield` mints `newYield = currentCollateralValue - _totalIssuedITry` to the yield receiver but never updates `_totalDLFUnderCustody`. Since `_totalIssuedITry` grows by `newYield` while collateral stays unchanged, the accounting invariant `collateralValue >= _totalIssuedITry` is preserved only because the minting itself was the "yield" — but the same NAV appreciation can be minted again and again after the yield receiver burns/recycles the tokens or when `previewAccumulatedYield` is queried repeatedly with no NAV change. Any subsequent integration that trusted `_totalIssuedITry` as backed supply will over-redeem.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (yield receiver) calls `processAccumulatedYield()` once to mint `X` yield. 2) Attacker transfers/sells the `X` iTRY to a whitelisted user. 3) Since `_totalIssuedITry` increased but collateral did not, the collateral backing ratio drops; the whitelisted user calls `redeemFor` for their original iTRY plus bought iTRY and drains more collateral than their fair share. 4) Remaining holders are undercollateralized.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral shortfall / protocol insolvency; the last redeemer cannot exit because `_totalDLFUnderCustody` is insufficient to cover `_totalIssuedITry`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Increment `_totalDLFUnderCustody` by the same yield amount (i.e., treat the yield as a realized collateral addition) OR track minted-but-not-backed supply separately and ensure redemptions cannot exceed `_totalDLFUnderCustody`.

hypotheses.title: FastAccessVault.rebalanceFunds lets anyone drain excess to custodian
hypotheses.description: `rebalanceFunds()` has no access restriction — any external caller can invoke it. When `currentBalance > targetBalance`, the excess is transferred to the `custodian` EOA/contract. A malicious user can repeatedly call this after depositing (via mintITRY) to force the vault to push liquidity out to the custodian at will, causing the buffer to sit at exactly `targetBalance` and hurting redemptions if the custodian is slow/offline. Also, if the admin later lowers `targetBufferPercentageBPS`, the caller's rebalance call will drain to the new smaller target.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Whitelisted user mints large amount of iTRY, growing vault balance > target. 2) Attacker (anyone) calls `rebalanceFunds()`. 3) Excess DLF is sent to the custodian, possibly to an address that does not return liquidity quickly, delaying user redemptions served from the buffer.
hypotheses.impact: Buffer forced to minimum; redemptions fall back to custodian path (non-instant), degrading user experience; possible denial of instant redemption at attacker-chosen times.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `rebalanceFunds()` to `onlyIssuer` or the vault owner (admin), or at least throttle callers.

hypotheses.title: StakediTry totalAssets underflows when unvested amount exceeds balance
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` returns `IERC20(asset()).balanceOf(address(this)) - getUnvestedAmount()`. If `getUnvestedAmount()` exceeds the contract's iTRY balance, this subtraction underflows and reverts. This can happen if the contract's iTRY balance is reduced (e.g., via `rescueTokens` for a different token, or if iTRY is somehow transferred out) while `vestingAmount` and `lastDistributionTimestamp` still imply a large unvested amount. More critically, `getUnvestedAmount()` is calculated as `(deltaT * vestingAmount) / vestingPeriod`. If `vestingAmount` is set via `transferInRewards` and then the contract's balance is reduced by a fast redeem or cooldown withdrawal that pulls more iTRY than expected, `totalAssets()` can revert. Since `totalAssets()` is used by ERC4626 functions like `convertToShares`, `convertToAssets`, `previewDeposit`, `previewRedeem`, `maxWithdraw`, `maxRedeem`, etc., a revert here bricks all vault operations.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker cannot directly cause this without a role, but a whitelisted user or the rewarder could trigger it. However, the attacker is untrusted. The only untrusted path is if a user can cause the contract's iTRY balance to drop below `getUnvestedAmount()`. This is not directly possible without a role. However, if `transferInRewards` is called and then a large cooldown withdrawal occurs, the balance could drop. But cooldown withdrawals move iTRY to the silo, not out of the contract. The silo holds the iTRY. So the contract's balance decreases. If `vestingAmount` is large and `getUnvestedAmount()` is large, and the contract's balance is reduced by cooldown withdrawals, `totalAssets()` can underflow. This is a real risk.
hypotheses.impact: All ERC4626 operations revert, freezing the vault. Users cannot deposit, withdraw, or redeem.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a saturating subtraction or check that `balanceOf(address(this)) >= getUnvestedAmount()` before subtracting, returning 0 if not.

hypotheses.title: wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake uses minAmountLD = assets with no slippage buffer
hypotheses.description: The return SendParam sets `minAmountLD: assets` (the exact amount) with no tolerance. LayerZero OFT applies a small dust removal (`sharedDecimals`), so the received amount on the spoke can be slightly less than `assets`, causing the OFT send to revert on the destination or the user to receive less than the minimum. There is no user-supplied slippage parameter; the value is hardcoded to the exact amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user initiates unstake; the hub computes `assets` and sends with `minAmountLD = assets`. Due to OFT dust removal or fee-on-transfer on the asset, the delivered amount is `assets - dust`, which is below `minAmountLD`, reverting the destination credit and stranding the user's iTRY on the hub composer.
hypotheses.impact: User's unstaked iTRY is stuck on the hub; user cannot retrieve it without admin intervention.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `minAmountLD` to a value slightly below `assets` (e.g., `assets * (10000 - slippageBps) / 10000`) or accept a user-supplied minimum.

hypotheses.title: _fastRedeem sets minAmountLD = assets, reverting on OFT dust
hypotheses.description: Same pattern as _handleUnstake: `_sendParam.minAmountLD = assets` where `assets` is the exact post-fee amount returned by `fastRedeemThroughComposer`. LayerZero OFT's `_removeDust` can reduce the delivered amount below `minAmountLD`, causing the destination credit to revert. The user's shares are already burned on the hub, so the assets are stranded.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user triggers FAST_REDEEM via the compose flow. The hub burns shares, computes `assets`, and sends with `minAmountLD = assets`. If dust removal or any fee reduces the delivered amount, the destination reverts and the user's iTRY is stuck on the hub composer.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (shares burned, assets stranded on hub).
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply a small slippage tolerance to `minAmountLD` (e.g., subtract dust or a configurable bps) instead of using the exact amount.

hypotheses.title: Mint fee rounding-up causes collateral accounting drift
hypotheses.description: `_calculateMintFee` returns `1` when the computed fee rounds down to zero (i.e., `dlfAmount * mintFeeInBPS < 10000`). However, `_transferIntoVault` only transfers `netDlfAmount` to the vault and `feeAmount` to the treasury, while `_totalDLFUnderCustody` is incremented by `netDlfAmount`. The user is charged `dlfAmount` (net + fee) but the protocol's tracked custody only reflects `netDlfAmount`. This is consistent, but the forced minimum fee of 1 wei means a user minting a tiny amount pays 1 wei of DLF as fee while receiving `(dlfAmount - 1) * navPrice / 1e18` iTRY. If `dlfAmount == 1` and `mintFeeInBPS > 0`, then `netDlfAmount = 0`, `iTRYAmount = 0`, and the function reverts with `ZeroAmount` after the fee was conceptually computed — but no transfer has occurred yet, so no loss. The real issue is that the minimum-fee-of-1 rule can make `netDlfAmount` zero for `dlfAmount == 1`, causing a revert rather than a graceful handling, and for `dlfAmount == 2` with high fee BPS, the user pays 1 wei fee and gets 1 wei of collateral credited. This is a dust-level accounting inconsistency, not a fund loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: A whitelisted user calls `mintITRY(1, 0)` with `mintFeeInBPS > 0`. `_calculateMintFee(1)` returns 1, so `netDlfAmount = 0`, `iTRYAmount = 0`, and the call reverts with `ZeroAmount`. No funds are lost, but the user cannot mint the smallest unit. For `dlfAmount = 2`, fee = 1, net = 1, iTRY = `1 * navPrice / 1e18`. The user effectively pays 50% fee on a 2-wei mint. This is a griefing/UX issue, not a theft.
hypotheses.impact: Dust-level minting is either impossible or incurs disproportionate fees. No loss of funds to an attacker; the protocol's accounting remains internally consistent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `feeAmount == 0 ? 1 : feeAmount` forced minimum, or require `dlfAmount` to be large enough that `netDlfAmount > 0` after fee deduction.

hypotheses.title: Redemption fee rounding-up can exceed gross amount for tiny redemptions
hypotheses.description: `_calculateRedemptionFee` returns `1` when the computed fee rounds down to zero. In `redeemFor`, `grossDlfAmount = iTRYAmount * 1e18 / navPrice`. If `grossDlfAmount == 1` and `redemptionFeeInBPS > 0`, then `feeAmount = 1` and `netDlfAmount = 0`. The code then checks `netDlfAmount < minAmountOut` (if `minAmountOut == 0`, this passes), burns the user's iTRY, and calls `_redeemFromVault` or `_redeemFromCustodian` with `receiveAmount = 0` and `feeAmount = 1`. `_redeemFromVault` calls `liquidityVault.processTransfer(receiver, 0)`, which reverts with `ZeroAmount` in `FastAccessVault.processTransfer`. So the transaction reverts, but the user's iTRY burn is rolled back. However, if `grossDlfAmount == 1` and the buffer path is taken, the revert is clean. The real issue is that for `grossDlfAmount == 1`, the user cannot redeem at all when fees are enabled, and for `grossDlfAmount == 2`, the user pays 1 wei fee and receives 1 wei. This is a dust-level DoS, not a fund loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: A whitelisted user calls `redeemITRY(1, 0)` with `redemptionFeeInBPS > 0` and `navPrice = 1e18`. `grossDlfAmount = 1`, `feeAmount = 1`, `netDlfAmount = 0`. The call reverts in `processTransfer` due to `ZeroAmount`. No funds are lost, but the user cannot redeem the smallest unit.
hypotheses.impact: Dust-level redemptions are impossible when fees are enabled. No loss of funds to an attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the forced minimum fee of 1, or require `grossDlfAmount > feeAmount` before proceeding.

hypotheses.title: wiTryVaultComposer _handleUnstake sends assets with minAmountLD = assets, causing revert on fee-on-transfer
hypotheses.description: In `_handleUnstake`, the composer calls `IStakediTryCrosschain(address(VAULT)).unstakeThroughComposer(user)` to get `assets`, then builds a `SendParam` with `amountLD: assets` and `minAmountLD: assets`. It then calls `_send(ASSET_OFT, _sendParam, address(this))`. If the `ASSET_OFT` is a fee-on-transfer token or if the LayerZero OFT applies a fee (e.g., `amountLD` is reduced by a fee), the actual amount received on the destination chain will be less than `assets`. Since `minAmountLD` is set to `assets`, the OFT's slippage check will revert. This means the unstake operation fails on the hub, and the user's funds are stuck. The `assets` amount is the gross amount from the vault, but the OFT may deduct a fee. The code does not account for this.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user initiates an unstake from the spoke chain. The hub receives the message, calls `unstakeThroughComposer`, and gets `assets`. The composer then tries to send `assets` with `minAmountLD = assets`. If the OFT has a fee, the send reverts. The user's unstaked iTRY is stuck in the composer, and the user cannot receive it on the spoke chain.
hypotheses.impact: The user's unstaked iTRY is stuck on the hub. The user loses the fees paid for the spoke→hub message and cannot recover the funds without admin intervention.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `minAmountLD` to a value that accounts for potential OFT fees, or use the OFT's `quoteSend` to determine the actual amount that will be received.

hypotheses.title: StakediTryCrosschain cooldown overwrites redeemer entitlement
hypotheses.description: In `_startComposerCooldown`, the contract first calls `_withdraw` (external interaction with the silo) and then writes `cooldowns[redeemer].cooldownEnd = cooldownEnd;` and `cooldowns[redeemer].underlyingAmount += uint152(assets);`. Because the cooldown end is overwritten rather than extended, if a redeemer already has an active cooldown with a later `cooldownEnd`, a subsequent composer-initiated cooldown for the same redeemer resets the timer to a shorter window. The underlying assets remain available to the redeemer earlier than the protocol intends, undermining the cooldown invariant.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker who controls a composer shares the composer role (trusted, but the bug affects user `redeemer`) or a whitelisted crosschain path invokes `cooldownSharesByComposer` twice for the same redeemer with a small share amount each time; the second call overwrites `cooldownEnd` to `block.timestamp + cooldownDuration`, letting the redeemer unstake the full accumulated amount before the original cooldown completion.
hypotheses.impact: Cooldown bypass and premature withdrawal of iTRY from the silo, weakening the protocol's liquidity/cooldown protection; accounting mismatch between intended cooldown duration and effective availability.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only set `cooldownEnd = max(existing, computed)` and never decrease an active `cooldownEnd`; also enforce a single active cooldown per redeemer.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger.unstake reverts on zero returnTripAllocation blocking unstake
hypotheses.description: The `unstake` function reverts with `InvalidReturnTripAllocation` when `returnTripAllocation == 0`. However, the return trip fee is quoted from `wiTryVaultComposer.quoteUnstakeReturn()`, which can legitimately return 0 in some LayerZero configurations (e.g., when the destination chain has zero messaging fee or when the OFT uses a zero-fee path). If the quoted return fee is 0, the user cannot unstake at all, permanently blocking the unstake flow for that configuration.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User calls `wiTryVaultComposer.quoteUnstakeReturn()` and receives `nativeFee == 0`. 2. User calls `unstake(0)` with the correct msg.value. 3. Transaction reverts with `InvalidReturnTripAllocation`. 4. User has no way to unstake because the only valid input is rejected.
hypotheses.impact: Users cannot unstake their wiTRY shares cross-chain when the return trip fee is zero, permanently locking funds in the vault from the user's perspective.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `returnTripAllocation == 0` revert, or allow a minimum non-zero value (e.g., 1 wei) to be passed when the quote returns zero.

hypotheses.title: wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake sends assets to user but refund goes to composer
hypotheses.description: In `_handleUnstake`, the function calls `_send(ASSET_OFT, _sendParam, address(this))`, meaning any excess LayerZero fees or refunds are sent to the composer contract itself, not the user. If the send fails or excess fees are refunded, those funds are stuck in the composer. While the composer has a `rescueToken` function, it is only callable by the owner, and there is no automatic mechanism to forward these refunds to the user. This can lead to stuck funds in the composer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User initiates unstake from spoke chain. 2. Hub processes unstake and sends assets back to user. 3. Excess LayerZero fees are refunded to the composer contract. 4. Funds remain stuck in the composer unless the owner manually rescues them.
hypotheses.impact: Stuck funds in the composer contract, requiring manual intervention by the owner to recover.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send refunds to the user or implement an automatic refund mechanism.

hypotheses.title: VaultComposerSync.lzCompose refunds to tx.origin enabling cross-chain replay/griefing
hypotheses.description: On compose failure, `_refund` sends the bridged tokens back to `tx.origin` on the source chain. `tx.origin` is not necessarily the original depositor; it is the EOA that initiated the transaction on the destination chain. An attacker can trigger a compose failure (e.g., by causing `handleCompose` to revert) and have the refund routed to an address they control, or grief legitimate users by forcing refunds to unintended recipients.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending compose message. 2) Attacker front-runs or triggers a condition that makes `handleCompose` revert (e.g., by manipulating vault state or sending a malformed `composeMsg`). 3) `_refund` sends the bridged tokens to `tx.origin` on the source chain. 4) If the attacker can influence `tx.origin` (e.g., via a contract they control that calls the endpoint), they capture the refund.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of bridged funds to an unintended recipient; griefing of legitimate users whose compose operations fail.
hypotheses.recommendation: Refund to the original `composeFrom` address (the depositor) rather than `tx.origin`, and validate that the refund recipient is the intended user.

hypotheses.title: StakediTryCrosschain._startComposerCooldown allows composer to overwrite redeemer cooldown
hypotheses.description: `_startComposerCooldown` sets `cooldowns[redeemer].cooldownEnd = cooldownEnd` and `cooldowns[redeemer].underlyingAmount += uint152(assets)`. If a redeemer already has an active cooldown, the composer can overwrite the `cooldownEnd` with a new value, potentially extending or shortening the existing cooldown. This allows a malicious or compromised composer to manipulate a user's cooldown timing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User initiates a cooldown via `cooldownShares` or `cooldownAssets`. 2) A composer with `COMPOSER_ROLE` calls `cooldownSharesByComposer` for the same redeemer. 3) `_startComposerCooldown` overwrites `cooldowns[redeemer].cooldownEnd` with a new timestamp, potentially extending the user's cooldown or allowing early withdrawal.
hypotheses.impact: User's cooldown period can be manipulated, leading to premature or delayed unstaking; potential loss of yield or forced lockup.
hypotheses.recommendation: Accumulate cooldown end times (e.g., `cooldownEnd = max(existing, new)`) or revert if a cooldown is already active for the redeemer.

hypotheses.title: processAccumulatedYield re-mints yield if yield tokens are burned or sent back
hypotheses.description: `newYield` is derived purely from `currentCollateralValue - _totalIssuedITry`. It does not track how much yield has been previously minted because the minted yield tokens themselves are counted in `_totalIssuedITry`. However, if the yield receiver's downstream staking vault (`StakediTry`) ever loses those tokens (e.g., slashing on a hypothetical redistribution, or the receiver burns them), `_totalIssuedITry` decreases while collateral stays the same, and the same NAV surplus is re-minted again.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls the yield receiver flow. 2) `processAccumulatedYield` mints `X`. 3) Yield receiver burns `X` iTRY via a mechanism that reduces `_totalIssuedITry` (e.g., iTry `redistributeLockedAmount` burn path). 4) Attacker calls `processAccumulatedYield` again and re-mints approximately `X`. 5) Repeat.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded inflation of iTRY supply beyond NAV backing; protocol becomes insolvent; existing holders diluted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a monotonically increasing `cumulativeYieldProcessed` and never mint yield exceeding `currentCollateralValue - _totalIssuedITry + cumulativeBurnedYield` with a serialized nonce, or derive yield from a stored checkpoint of NAV rather than the live difference.

hypotheses.title: Cooldown timestamp reset allows user to extend cooldown advantageously
hypotheses.description: Each `cooldownAssets`/`cooldownShares` call overwrites `cooldowns[msg.sender].cooldownEnd` with `block.timestamp + cooldownDuration` even if a previous cooldown for the same user is mid-flight. Because `underlyingAmount` is additive, a user who is near the end of a cooldown can call the function a second time with a tiny additional amount, resetting the cooldown timer for the entirety of the silo balance. This is by design in Ethena, but is combined with `unstake()` being all-or-nothing so the user is forced to `cooldownAssets` again with only a tiny amount, forever extending the cooldown for the accumulated silo balance and enabling griefing/timing games against integrations that rely on predictable cooldown release.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User starts cooldown with a large `assets`. 2) Just before `cooldownEnd`, user calls `cooldownAssets(1 wei)` (or smallest possible) — timer resets. 3) User repeats indefinitely, locking their own silo accounting in a specific epoch, potentially interfering with composer-initiated cooldowns that write to the same `cooldowns[receiver]` slot.
hypotheses.impact: Cooldown state corruption for crosschain composers; `unstakeThroughComposer` reverts because `cooldownEnd` was silently pushed forward by a prior user call, or vice versa — `underlyingAmount` is augmented incorrectly leading to wrong accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject `cooldownAssets`/`cooldownShares` when an existing cooldown is active (`userCooldown.underlyingAmount > 0 && block.timestamp < userCooldown.cooldownEnd`), or use max of existing/new end times instead of overwrite.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger refunds to msg.sender but on hub user may lose funds
hypotheses.description: The hub-side `wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake` uses `_origin.srcEid` and `unstakeMsg.user` (encoded from spoke as `msg.sender`) to send iTRY back. But the return send's refund address is `address(this)` (the composer), and LayerZero refunds for the hub→spoke leg go back to the composer, not the user. If the destination send reverts or if there's excess native fee, refunds accumulate on the composer and are only recoverable via owner-only `rescueToken`. Additionally, on spoke→hub dispatch, only `msg.sender` on the spoke is captured as the user — if the user interacts through a contract or smart wallet (e.g., a `UnstakeMessenger` caller from a multisig), refunds and the return trip are pinned to that caller, and the end user cannot redirect.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User A on spoke invokes `unstake()` via a smart-contract wallet. 2) `msg.sender` = smart wallet, encoded as user in payload. 3) On hub, iTRY is returned to `smart wallet`. Not exploitable by an untrusted third party but is a state-consistency issue around who the end recipient should be. Additionally, any LayerZero dust refunded to the composer on the hub is stuck unless the owner rescues it.
hypotheses.impact: Funds (iTRY return leg + dust native) can be effectively frozen on the composer if the user cannot call hub-side owner functions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass an explicit `refundAddress`/`recipient` in the `UnstakeMessage`, and forward LayerZero surplus native refunds to that recipient rather than `address(this)`.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger.unstake allows arbitrary returnTripAllocation griefing
hypotheses.description: `unstake(uint256 returnTripAllocation)` accepts any nonzero `returnTripAllocation` from the caller and embeds it as native value forwarded to the hub via `addExecutorLzReceiveOption`. The hub's `_handleUnstake` then calls `unstakeThroughComposer(user)` where `user` is `msg.sender` on the spoke. There is no check that the caller actually owns wiTRY shares on the hub, nor that `returnTripAllocation` matches the quoted return fee. An attacker can spam `unstake` with a huge `returnTripAllocation` (paying the correspondingly large spoke fee) to force the hub composer to attempt unstaking for arbitrary addresses, and the hub will forward the full `returnTripAllocation` as native value to the composer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `unstake{value: hugeFee}(hugeReturnTripAllocation)` from an address with no wiTRY position. 2) Hub `_handleUnstake` calls `unstakeThroughComposer(attacker)` which reverts with `NoAssetsToUnstake` (or `InvalidCooldown`). 3) The revert consumes the forwarded native value on the hub side; the attacker has burned their own funds but can also grief by targeting addresses that do have cooldowns, forcing premature unstake attempts.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / wasted gas and native value; potential forced unstake of other users' cooldowns if the attacker can spoof the `user` field (they cannot, since it's `msg.sender`), but the lack of validation on `returnTripAllocation` allows overpayment and hub-side revert loops.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `returnTripAllocation` against a reasonable bound or against the quoted return fee, and consider requiring the caller to have a corresponding hub-side position before dispatching.

hypotheses.title: wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake re-enters vault without reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `_handleUnstake` decodes `unstakeMsg.user` from the LayerZero message and calls `IStakediTryCrosschain(VAULT).unstakeThroughComposer(user)` before sending `ASSET_OFT`. There is no `nonReentrant` on the composer `_lzReceive` path, and the vault `unstakeThroughComposer` only enforces its own `nonReentrant` per call. If the OFT asset token or vault implementation ever invokes a hook into the composer (or if the same `_lzReceive` path can be triggered concurrently via a crafted composition), state on the composer is not protected. Because the funds flow (silo withdraw → composer → OFT send) happens before any local accounting on the composer, a reentrant call could drain silo balances again before the first send settles.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker composes a LayerZero message routed to `handleCompose`/`_lzReceive` such that the asset OFT or the silo hook re-enters `lzCompose`/`_lzReceive` (or triggers an external contract that reenters), issuing a second `unstakeThroughComposer` for the same receiver before the first transfer completes.
hypotheses.impact: Double-withdrawal from the silo / iTRY vault, insolvency of the vault, loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to composer entrypoints that touch the vault and OFT (`lzCompose`, `handleCompose`, `_handleUnstake`), and perform state bookkeeping before external calls.

hypotheses.title: iTryTokenOFT._beforeTokenTransfer allows minter to bypass blacklist on mint
hypotheses.description: In `FULLY_ENABLED` state, the mint branch checks `!blacklisted[to]`, but the redeem branch checks `!blacklisted[from]` and `to == address(0)`. The minter (LayerZero endpoint) can mint to a blacklisted address if the `to` check is bypassed via a crafted message, or the minter can be tricked into minting to a blacklisted recipient. More critically, the `redistributeLockedAmount` function burns from a blacklisted address and mints to a non-blacklisted address, but the `_beforeTokenTransfer` hook does not enforce that `msg.sender == owner()` for the mint branch when `from == address(0)`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets a blacklisted address whitelisted or finds a path where the minter mints to a blacklisted address. 2) The mint branch allows it because `!blacklisted[to]` is checked, but if `to` is blacklisted, the mint reverts. 3) However, the `redistributeLockedAmount` function can be called by the owner to move funds from a blacklisted address to a non-blacklisted address, bypassing the blacklist intent.
hypotheses.impact: Blacklisted addresses can receive or move funds, defeating the blacklist mechanism.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce that `msg.sender == owner()` for the redistribute mint branch and ensure the minter cannot mint to blacklisted addresses.

hypotheses.title: FastAccessVault.processTransfer bypasses _totalDLFUnderCustody accounting revert
hypotheses.description: `_redeemFromVault` decrements `_totalDLFUnderCustody` by `receiveAmount + feeAmount` and then calls `liquidityVault.processTransfer`. If the vault doesn't actually hold `grossDlfAmount` (e.g., because `rebalanceFunds` previously pushed excess to the custodian), the vault's internal check `currentBalance < _amount` reverts and the whole tx reverts — good. However, the buffer-balance check `bufferBalance >= grossDlfAmount` uses `getAvailableBalance()` (the vault's balance), but `_totalDLFUnderCustody` also includes collateral sitting at the custodian. When custodian-held collateral exists, this path silently succeeds while custodian-side collateral is never decremented, so subsequent custodian-based redemptions can over-withdraw because accounting and physical custody diverge.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Whitelisted user mints with DLF, collateral goes to vault. 2) Anyone calls `rebalanceFunds` to move excess to custodian. 3) Whitelisted user redeems and the buffer still has enough for gross, draining the vault. 4) Another user redeems; buffer is now short; `_redeemFromCustodian` is used but the custodian may have already received the excess earlier via rebalance, so `_totalDLFUnderCustody` decrement diverges from actual custodian balance and later redemptions emit transfer requests for assets that don't exist off-chain.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain custodian instructed to transfer more than it holds → redemptions fail off-chain, users' iTRY burned but no DLF received; wrong `_totalDLFUnderCustody`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cross-check `_totalDLFUnderCustody` against vault balance + custodian-reported balance before decrement, or require custodian reconciliation accounting.

hypotheses.title: Type inference allows untrusted user to trigger zero amount fast redeem
hypotheses.description: The function computes `shares = previewWithdraw(assets)` but does not check for zero shares when `assets` is very small relative to the vault's ratio (e.g., after fee has been subtracted or in extreme ratio situations). The fee returned is computed on `assets`, and after subtracting it `assets - feeAssets` can be 0 while the call still bills fees and emits an event. This isn't an owner-only issue because it can be triggered by a composer calling the function.
hypotheses.attackPath: Composer calls `fastWithdrawThroughComposer(1, receiver, owner)` with a dust `assets`. Since `previewWithdraw(1)` rounds to 0, `_withdraw` may be called with zero shares (the base's `notZero` check catches this in some paths) — but at the composer entry-point, `maxWithdraw(composer) >= 1` may pass and the flow proceeds to `_redeemWithFee`, which has an `InvalidAmount` check but only when feeAssets==0, so it can succeed with dust accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting/emissions, minor loss via fee split inconsistency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an explicit `if (shares == 0) revert InvalidAmount();` after `previewWithdraw` in `fastWithdrawThroughComposer`.

hypotheses.title: iTryIssuer mint accounting ignores fee so previewMint vs mint consistent but yield preview broken
hypotheses.description: `_totalDLFUnderCustody` is incremented only by the net DLF amount; the fee is transferred to the treasury but not added to collateral under custody, which is consistent for accounting. However, `previewAccumulatedYield` compares `_totalDLFUnderCustody * navPrice / 1e18` to `_totalIssuedITry`. Because both mint and redeem adjust both sides, an attacker (any whitelisted user) can call mint right before `processAccumulatedYield` to manipulate the recorded ratio and either inflate or deflate reported yield, affecting real yieldReceiver minted amount. The state divergence is due to the fee being moved out of the collateral system entirely (to treasury) while iTRY issued is still for the net amount; rounding then causes yield to be over/under stated depending on user's own rounding direction.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Whitelisted user calls `mintITRY(1, 0)` with a fee >0. 2) `_totalIssuedITry` increments by floor(1*nav/1e18) = 0? No — nav may be >1e18 so it may mint dust. 3) Repeatedly call to nudge `_totalIssuedITry` vs `_totalDLFUnderCustody`. 4) Call `processAccumulatedYield` in the same block if granted distributor role — but attacker lacks role, so yield snapshot cannot be forced. Partial only; yield snapshot happens by trusted keeper timing. Confidence lowered.
hypotheses.impact: Manipulation of reported yield; potential over-mint to yieldReceiver depending on rounding direction.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track fee amounts within the collateral accounting or snapshot the ratio at yield processing time with a guarded TWAP.

hypotheses.title: wiTryOFT.redistributeBlackListedFunds can be front-run by blacklisted user
hypotheses.description: `redistributeBlackListedFunds` temporarily sets `blackList[_from] = false`, calls `_transfer(_from, owner(), _amount)`, then restores the flag. During the `_transfer` call, `_beforeTokenTransfer` checks `blackList[_from]` which is now false, so the transfer succeeds. However, if `_from` is a contract with a hook (or if the owner is a contract), the blacklisted user can re-enter or front-run the owner's transaction to move funds first. More directly, the blacklisted user can front-run the owner's `redistributeBlackListedFunds` tx by transferring their balance to a non-blacklisted address — but `_beforeTokenTransfer` blocks that. The real issue is that the temporary un-blacklist window is observable and the owner's tx can be front-run by the blacklisted user calling `updateBlackList` if they somehow have the blackLister role — which they don't. The concrete flaw is that `_transfer` is called while the flag is false, and if `_from` is a malicious contract, its `_beforeTokenTransfer` override (if any) or a reentrant call could exploit the window.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Blacklisted user deploys a contract at their address (or uses an existing contract) that re-enters `updateBlackList` or `_transfer` during the owner's `redistributeBlackListedFunds` call. 2) During the temporary un-blacklist, the attacker moves funds to a safe address before the owner's transfer completes.
hypotheses.impact: Blacklisted funds escape the redistribution mechanism, defeating the blacklist's purpose.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a dedicated internal transfer path that bypasses the blacklist check without mutating state, or perform the transfer via a `_transfer` override that explicitly allows the owner-initiated redistribution.

hypotheses.title: _redeemWithFee performs two _withdraw calls with stale share accounting
hypotheses.description: `_redeemWithFee` computes `feeShares = previewWithdraw(feeAssets)` and `netShares = shares - feeShares` before calling `_withdraw` twice on the same vault. Since `_withdraw` mutates totalSupply and asset balance between the two calls, the second `_withdraw` uses a `netShares` value derived from pre-mutation state, and the ERC4626 rounding between `previewWithdraw` and actual burn can diverge. In extreme rounding/configurations the fee portion may not match the assets pulled, leaving the vault accounting inconsistent and potentially allowing value extraction.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted user calls `fastRedeem` / `fastWithdraw` (or the composer version) repeatedly to exploit rounding where `feeShares` is computed with a stale asset/share ratio; the second `_withdraw` burns less/more shares than intended and shifts the loss to other stakers.
hypotheses.impact: Accounting drift in the vault, potential under/over-collection of fees, and value leakage from remaining shareholders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `netShares = shares - feeShares` and perform a single combined accounting step, or recompute `netShares` after the first `_withdraw` using fresh `previewWithdraw`.

hypotheses.title: UnstakeMessenger.unstake trusts caller-supplied returnTripAllocation
hypotheses.description: `unstake(returnTripAllocation)` embeds the user-provided `returnTripAllocation` directly into the LayerZero options via `addExecutorLzReceiveOption(LZ_RECEIVE_GAS, uint128(returnTripAllocation))` and uses `msg.value` only to pay the resulting quote. The value is not bounded anywhere in the messenger; a user can set `returnTripAllocation` to any uint128 value, and the hub side `wiTryVaultComposer._handleUnstake` will forward it. Combined with `_send` refunds (`address(this)`) on the composer, mismatched options/msg.value can leave stuck native value or cause the hub leg to over/under-pay gas on the return hop.
hypotheses.attackPath: User calls `quoteUnstakeWithReturnValue` with an arbitrary `returnTripValue`, sends exactly the quoted fee, and the return trip on the hub is executed with a fabricated native value; if the hub leg over-credits or fails, `wiTryVaultComposer` accumulates or misroutes funds that the user can later drain through `rescueToken`-like paths only available to owner — or funds get stranded.
hypotheses.impact: Potential loss of native gas funds on hub, denial of return leg if option value deviates from expected, or mis-accounting of bridged refunds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound `returnTripAllocation` on the spoke against the queried return fee plus a tight buffer, and derive it from a trusted quote instead of trusting user input blindly.

hypotheses.title: iTryIssuer.redeemFor burns user tokens before buffer/custodian selection
hypotheses.description: `redeemFor` calls `_burn(msg.sender, iTRYAmount)` before checking `liquidityVault.getAvailableBalance()` and before invoking `_redeemFromVault` / `_redeemFromCustodian`. Any reentrancy or state change triggered by the burn (e.g., a hook in a customized iTRY token implementation) occurs before the DLF accounting (`_totalDLFUnderCustody`, oracle reads) is finalized, and the buffer balance check uses a value fetched after the burn. If the user token has transfer hooks or the vault shares are not fully isolated, the ordering allows observing mutated total supply with stale collateral assumptions.
hypotheses.attackPath: An external actor with WHITELISTED_USER_ROLE (or social-engineered moderator) issues `redeemFor` and reenters via a token hook (or via a callback from `processTransfer` before accounting settles) to trigger a second redeem that reads the just-updated buffer balance and mis-computes the source of funds.
hypotheses.impact: Double redemption, misattribution of buffer vs custodian redemption, incorrect `_totalDLFUnderCustody` accounting, potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Follow strict CEI: determine source of funds and decrement accounting before burning/sending, and add `nonReentrant` around vault interaction sequence.

hypotheses.title: FastAccessVault.rebalanceFunds sends excess to custodian with no reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `rebalanceFunds()` computes excess from `_vaultToken.balanceOf(address(this))` and then transfers to the `custodian` with no `nonReentrant` modifier. If the vault token (DLF) has transfer hooks (ERC777-like) or the custodian is a contract that reenters, the attacker can reenter `processTransfer`/`rebalanceFunds` again while `balanceOf` still reflects the pre-transfer state, causing multiple excess transfers.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (anyone can call `rebalanceFunds`) triggers a transfer to a malicious custodian contract (if custodian were untrusted) or causes the vault token to invoke a callback, reentering `rebalanceFunds` to drain the buffer before the balance decreases.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of FastAccessVault buffer, leaving the protocol without instant-redeem liquidity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `rebalanceFunds` and update accounting prior to the transfer.

hypotheses.title: VaultComposerSync._refund can be called repeatedly by anyone via failed compose
hypotheses.description: `lzCompose` is invoked by the endpoint with `msg.value` set by whoever retries the compose. If `handleCompose` reverts with anything other than `InsufficientMsgValue`, the catch block calls `_refund` which sends the tokens back to the original sender. However, because the try/catch swallows reverts and repeatedly calls `_refund`, an attacker can craft a compose message that deliberately reverts in `handleCompose` after the OFT has already credited this composer (e.g., by making `_deposit`/`deposit` fail via an ERC4626 that reverts on `maxDeposit` conditions), causing the OFT credit to be refunded AND leaving the attacker with the original bridged amount. Also `_refund` is not guarded against being executed multiple times for the same `_guid`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends OFT shares cross-chain to composer with a composeMsg designed to revert in `handleCompose` (e.g., slippage/minOut impossible). 2) `lzCompose` credits composer via OFT, then catch triggers `_refund`, sending the shares back. 3) Endpoint re-delivers the same message (it wasn't marked delivered due to revert in `lzCompose` from `InsufficientMsgValue` path, or via retry) and attacker repeats. 4) Attacker can wedge share accounting if any state in the composer or vault was mutated before revert.
hypotheses.impact: Refund can be claimed multiple times against the same inbound amount if compose can be re-triggered; vault accounting mismatch due to shares not fully returned to vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track processed `guid`s in a `mapping(bytes32 => bool)` and short-circuit duplicate `lzCompose` calls, or move state mutations after refund logic.

hypotheses.title: Fast redeem fee charged twice against same shares
hypotheses.description: `_redeemWithFee` computes `feeShares = previewWithdraw(feeAssets)` and `netShares = shares - feeShares`, then performs two `_withdraw` calls. Because `_withdraw` is `nonReentrant` on the base but not on the fee sub-call, and `previewWithdraw` uses the current vault ratio, the two `_withdraw` calls can settle at slightly different effective asset/share prices if any external hook or state change occurs between them; more importantly, `previewWithdraw(feeAssets)` may round up so that `feeShares > (shares * fee / BASIS_POINTS)`, meaning the treasury takes more shares than the stated fee and the user receives less. In addition, if `previewWithdraw` returns 0 for a small fee, `netShares == shares` and the fee user pays is zero assets while accounting decrements remain skewed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses `fastRedeem` with a very small share amount near `MIN_SHARES` boundary. 2) `previewWithdraw(feeAssets)` returns a value that, combined with `_withdraw`'s internal rounding, charges more than `fastRedeemFeeInBPS` to treasury (charging the user more than advertised). 3) Conversely with a large amount, the attacker can drive `netShares` such that `_withdraw` on the net portion reverts due to `MIN_SHARES` violation, forcing fee portion to still be taken in earlier tx if share accounting is mutated between calls.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair fee extraction; users may lose more shares than advertised; possible griefing DoS of fast redeem for accounts near the MIN_SHARES boundary.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `netAssets` first, then perform a single `_withdraw` for the total and separately transfer the fee from the composer (or use `previewWithdraw` on total to derive fee shares consistently with rounding direction favoring the user).
